strengths: Clear and timely problem formalization: the paper establishes global-scale audio geolocation as a new research task, adapting evaluation protocols (Haversine median error, percentage-at-threshold) from image geolocation in a sensible way.

Comprehensive experimental design: the paper benchmarks regression, classification (including hierarchical H3 grids), explicit species-range-based geolocation, and retrieval approaches, and provides upper-bound 'species oracle' experiments that meaningfully contextualize achievable performance (97.8% region accuracy with full checklists vs. 17.2% for the best end-to-end model).

The proposed AG-CLIP method is simple but well-motivated: adding a SINR-checklist auxiliary loss to a GeoCLIP-style retrieval model yields the best audio-based performance across scales, and the ablations (audio encoders, location encoders, pooling strategies, location galleries in Table A1) are thorough.

New dataset contribution (XCDC): the dawn-chorus benchmark is a thoughtful probe of the species-richness hypothesis, and the negative result (models achieve only ~2.5-5.3% region accuracy on species-rich audio despite a 25.8% oracle ceiling) is honestly reported and analytically useful — it clearly delineates the gap between the information available in soundscapes and current models' ability to exploit it.

The spatiotemporal aggregation analysis (Table 4) provides a useful practical finding: grouping recordings across a year within 253 km^2 nearly doubles region accuracy (17.2% to 30.4%), with the species-count distributions in the right panel supporting the interpretation.
Good reproducibility posture: benchmark and codebase are released, hyperparameters and compute details are documented (Appendix A.5, A.13), and multi-run means/std are reported.
Honest treatment of limitations, including geographic bias in iNatSounds and privacy risks of geolocation technology, in the conclusion.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited: AG-CLIP is essentially GeoCLIP applied to spectrograms plus a BCE checklist auxiliary loss; the location encoder is frozen from GeoCLIP, and the core contribution is the benchmark and analysis rather than a new technique.

Absolute performance is modest, and the improvements of AG-CLIP over baselines are small at some scales (e.g., region 17.2% vs. hierarchical classification 16.6%); the checklist auxiliary loss contributes only 2.7% at the continent level and nothing at finer scales (Table 2b).

The species oracle experiments rely on checklists constructed from SINR-predicted range maps at the oracle location; since SINR was trained on much larger occurrence corpora, the oracle upper bound may overstate what audio-derived species signals could achieve, and this confound is acknowledged but not fully quantified.

The headline species-richness hypothesis is not validated by the models: on XCDC, all model-based approaches perform roughly at the level of a single-species signal, and the paper attributes this to distribution shift without additional experiments (e.g., fine-tuning or domain adaptation on species-rich audio) that would test this explanation.

The multimodal geo-forensics section (Sec. 5.4) is anecdotal: only four hand-selected movie scenes, chosen because viewers already flagged them, so the 'confirmation' of modality inconsistency carries little evidential weight.

Retrieval galleries constructed from the training-set location distribution (used for the main results) could inflate city/region-level accuracy relative to a uniform-land gallery (6.4% vs 1.3-1.6% at city level in Table A1); main-table comparisons to GeoCLAP/Taxabind using different galleries warrant more caution in interpretation.

Several key analyses (spatial variation, XCDC evaluation) are confounded by the severe geographic and density imbalance of iNatSounds; the paper notes the bias but does not conduct bias-controlled or region-stratified evaluation.

strengths: The paper formalizes a new task (global-scale natural audio geolocation) and releases a benchmark (iNatSounds splits plus a new dawn-chorus dataset, XCDC) with a codebase, which is a useful resource for an underexplored area.

The experimental design is unusually thorough for a benchmark paper: naive baselines, oracle species checklists as upper bounds, regression/classification/retrieval families, ablations over audio encoders, location encoders, pooling, and location galleries (Table A1), repeated runs with std, and spatial error analysis (Fig. 3).

The oracle experiments are a nice framing device: they quantify the value of species information (e.g., 97.8% region accuracy with full checklists vs. 37.6% with 10 species) and honestly expose the gap between oracle and realistic model performance.

The paper is candid about limitations: geographic bias of iNatSounds toward Western countries, the distribution shift on XCDC, the fact that species oracles are unrealistic, and privacy implications of audio geolocation.
The observations that spatiotemporal aggregation improves accuracy (17.2% -> 30.4% region) and that models fail to exploit multi-species soundscapes on XCDC are genuinely informative for future work.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited. The proposed method, AG-CLIP, is essentially GeoCLIP with a MobileNetV3 spectrogram encoder and an auxiliary BCE checklist head (weight 0.01); the checklist loss accounts for only ~2.7% continent-level gain (Table 2b), so the core contribution rests on the benchmark rather than a substantive methodological advance.

Potential evaluation leakage in the retrieval setup: the default gallery is the training set's own locations (Table 1 and A1), which aligns the gallery with the test distribution and may inflate city/region accuracy relative to the uniform/land galleries (region 17.4% vs 15.0-15.4%). While the gallery ablation mitigates this, the headline numbers in Table 1 use the most favorable gallery, and the dependence of retrieval-style geolocation on gallery composition is a confound not fully resolved.

Absolute performance is weak: median error ~1082 km and only 6.4% city / 17.2% region accuracy, so the practical utility of the best method is unclear; the paper does not establish a meaningful operating point for any application.

The multimodal geo-forensics section (Sec. 5.4, Fig. 4) is anecdotal: only four cherry-picked movie scenes, selected because viewers already flagged mismatches, with no quantitative evaluation, controls, or failure analysis. As a contribution it adds little beyond anecdote and inflates the claimed contribution list.

Dataset biases are acknowledged but not addressed: iNatSounds is geographically skewed, and performance concentrates in data-rich regions (Fig. 3 right). The XCDC evaluation (n=576 recordings) is small, and the species richness of XCDC groups (Table 4 right) suggests some aggregation conditions are dominated by single-species groups, weakening the interpretation.

The 'first study addressing global-scale geolocation of natural audio' claim needs more careful qualification given prior audio/multimodal geolocation work the authors themselves cite (e.g., Foley et al. on radio broadcasts, Friedland et al.), and the significance of the contribution is niche relative to ICML's main track.

Several methodological details are under-justified, e.g., the SINR 0.1 binarization threshold for checklists, and why a hierarchical classifier (0->1->2) trained independently without conditioning performs as reported; reproducibility depends heavily on the promised code release.

strengths: First study to formalize and benchmark global-scale audio geolocation on natural sound; this fills a genuine gap between image geolocation and soundscape mapping, and the paper positions itself well against both literatures (Sec. 2).

Comprehensive experimental design: the paper systematically compares regression, classification (including hierarchical H3 grids), species-range-based geolocation, and retrieval approaches, and the oracle experiments with full/corrupted species checklists (Table 1) provide valuable upper bounds that contextualize what end-to-end models can achieve.

AG-CLIP is a sensible, well-motivated extension of GeoCLIP: the auxiliary SINR checklist prediction loss encourages the encoder to exploit background/ambient species cues, and ablations (Table 2) isolate the contribution of each design choice (audio encoder, location encoder, BCE loss weight, pooling strategy).

The XCDC dawn-chorus benchmark (Sec. 5.3) and the spatiotemporal aggregation study (Table 4) probe scientifically interesting questions about multi-species signals and demonstrate an honest negative result: current models fail to exploit species-rich soundscapes (≤5.3% region accuracy vs. 25.8% with oracle species), which is itself an informative finding.

Thorough supplemental material: gallery ablations (Table A1), implementation and hyperparameter details, compute resources, additional visualizations with links to source observations, and reproducibility support (benchmark + codebase).
Honest treatment of limitations and ethics: the conclusion explicitly discusses geographic bias in iNatSounds and privacy risks of audio geolocation, without overstating capabilities.
weaknesses: The proposed method is a relatively modest engineering increment over GeoCLIP (a checklist decoder plus weighted BCE loss); the improvement is +2.7% at continent level with diminishing gains at finer scales, and absolute performance remains low (city 6.4%, region 17.2%), so the contribution leans heavily on the benchmark and analysis rather than a strong new technique.

Baseline fairness concerns: GeoCLAP and Taxabind are evaluated strictly off-the-shelf without any adaptation or fine-tuning on iNatSounds, while AG-CLIP is trained on it; the comparison in Table 1 therefore partly measures domain match rather than method quality. Fine-tuning these baselines would strengthen claims of superiority.

Potential circularity in the species signal: the checklists that supervise AG-CLIP and the 'Species Ranges' baselines are all derived from SINR, which is itself trained on occurrence data; how much of the species-range advantage reflects independent geographic information versus overlap with iNatSounds/iNaturalist data sources is not analyzed.

Retrieval results depend on the location gallery: the train-set gallery outperforms uniform galleries by a noticeable margin (Table A1, region 17.4% vs 15.0%), meaning reported numbers partly reflect test-time access to the training location distribution; this is ablated but the headline numbers use the most favorable gallery.

XCDC is small (576 recordings) and evaluated only zero-shot from iNatSounds-trained models, so the 'species-rich audio' conclusions (Sec. 5.3) conflate dataset shift with the multi-species hypothesis; the claimed gap would be more convincing with a training experiment on species-rich data (which the authors defer to future work).

The multimodal geo-forensics section (Sec. 5.4) is purely anecdotal: four hand-picked movie scenes, no quantitative protocol, no negative controls (e.g., unflagged scenes), and cherry-picked stimuli; it is presented as a case study but the evidential value is limited.

Absolute usefulness of the artifact is constrained by the acknowledged geographic bias of iNatSounds toward the Northern Hemisphere/Western countries, which limits both what the models learn and what the benchmark can measure; the paper acknowledges this but does not offer mitigation (e.g., region-stratified evaluation).
The benchmark and codebase release links appear as empty placeholders in the text (Sec. 1 and Appendix A), which currently weakens reproducibility claims as submitted.
